slides.heading: The Rise of Humanoid Robots
slides.body: From factory floors to everyday life — machines are finally walking among us

slides.heading: Why Now?
slides.body: A convergence of AI breakthroughs, cheaper actuators, and better batteries has made humanoid robots economically viable for the first time. The cost of building a capable humanoid has dropped by over 80% since 2020.

slides.heading: The Leading Players
slides.body: Tesla Optimus, Figure AI, Agility Robotics, and Boston Dynamics lead the race. Each takes a different approach — from AI-first training to biomechanical design — competing for dominance in a market projected to reach $150 billion by 2035.

slides.heading: Learning to Move Like Humans
slides.body: Modern humanoids learn movement through reinforcement learning in simulated environments. They practice millions of virtual hours — walking, grasping, recovering from falls — before ever touching the real world, dramatically cutting development time.

slides.heading: Working Alongside People
slides.body: Humanoid robots are already operating in Amazon warehouses, BMW factories, and hospital supply rooms. Their human-like form lets them use existing tools and navigate spaces built for people — no costly facility redesign required.

slides.heading: The Dexterity Problem
slides.body: Hands remain the hardest challenge. Human fingers can apply 1 newton of force or 100 — and feel the difference. Today's robot hands struggle with tasks like picking a strawberry without crushing it, a problem researchers call the 'manipulation gap.'

slides.heading: Safety and Trust
slides.body: Regulators in the US, EU, and Japan are scrambling to create frameworks for human-robot coexistence. Key questions: How should a robot behave when it makes a mistake? Who is liable when a humanoid injures someone? These answers will shape the entire industry.

slides.heading: Economic Impact
slides.body: Economists estimate humanoid robots could add $4–7 trillion to global GDP by 2040 by addressing labor shortages in manufacturing, logistics, and elder care. However, up to 14% of current jobs could be displaced, requiring major workforce transition programs.

slides.heading: The Home Frontier
slides.body: The next big target is the home market. Companies are racing to build a robot that can load dishwashers, fold laundry, and assist elderly people with mobility. A capable home assistant robot could outsell smartphones within a decade.

slides.heading: A New Kind of Colleague
slides.body: Humanoid robots won't replace humanity — they'll extend it. The question isn't whether they'll arrive, but how quickly we shape the rules that govern them. The age of humanoid machines has begun.
